notes.title: Post Mortem - Two Years After the Premiere of We. The Refugees
notes.notes:
[h1]Two Years Later: What We Got Right, What We Got Wrong, and What We Learned[/h1]

When we started working on [i]We. The Refugees: Ticket to Europe[/i], we didn’t have a publisher, a studio, or even a real budget. Just an idea, a lot of questions, and more ambition than we probably should’ve had. Two years after release, the game was nominated to and received international awards, has earned a dedicated niche following, and a respectable 83% positive rating on Steam — but financially, it hasn’t been the success we hoped for.

This post mortem is a look behind the curtain: how the game was born, how we pulled it off with limited resources, what mistakes we made (some of them big), and what we’d do differently next time. It’s part reflection, part open notebook — for fellow devs, curious players, and anyone wondering what it really takes to make a politically charged narrative game in 2020s Europe.

Let’s start at the beginning.

[h1]The Origins of the Game[/h1]

The idea behind [i]We. The Refugees [/i]goes back to 2014–2015, when news about the emerging refugee crisis began making global headlines. At the time, the two co-founders of Act Zero — Jędrzej Napiecek and Maciej Stańczyk — were QA testers working on [i]The Witcher 3[/i] at Testronic. During coffee breaks, they’d talk about their desire to create something of their own: a narrative-driven game with a message. They were particularly inspired by [i]This War of Mine[/i] from 11 bit studios — one of the first widely recognized examples of a so-called "meaningful game." All of these ingredients became the base for the cocktail that would eventually become our first game. 

At first, the project was just a modest side hustle — an attempt to create a game about refugees that could help players better understand a complex issue. Over the next few years, we researched the topic, built a small team, and searched for funding. Eventually, we secured a micro-budget from a little-known publisher (who soon disappeared from the industry). That collaboration didn’t last long, but it gave us enough momentum to build a very bad prototype and organize a research trip to refugee camps on the Greek island of Lesbos.

That trip changed everything. It made us realize how little we truly understood — even after years of preparation. The contrast between our secondhand knowledge and the reality on the ground was jarring. That confrontation became a defining theme of the game. We restructured the narrative around it: not as a refugee survival simulator, but as a story about someone trying — and often failing — to understand. In the new version, the player steps into the shoes of an amateur journalist at the start of his career. You can learn more about it in the [url=https://youtu.be/Icb5bEAVwag?si=k6EdyYM1nys_ZeAm]documentary film[/url] showcasing our development and creative process.   

But for a moment we have no money to continue the development of [i]We. The Refugees[/i]. For the next year and a half, the studio kept itself afloat with contract work — mainly developing simulator games for companies in the PlayWay group — while we continued our hunt for funding. Finally, in 2019, we received an EU grant to build the game, along with a companion comic book and board game on the same subject. From the first conversation over coffee to actual financing, the road took about five years.

[h1]Budget and Production[/h1]

The EU grant we received totaled 425,000 PLN — roughly $100,000. But that sum had to stretch across three different projects: a video game, a board game, and a comic book. While some costs overlapped — particularly in visual development — we estimate that [b]the actual budget allocated to the [i]We. The Refugees[/i] video game was somewhere in the range of $70,000–$80,000[/b].

The production timeline stretched from May 2020 to May 2023 — three full years. That’s a long time for an indie game of this size, but the reasons were clear:

First, the script was enormous — around 300,000 words, or roughly two-thirds the length of [i]The Witcher 3[/i]’s narrative. Writing alone took nearly 20 months.

Second, the budget didn’t allow for a full-time team. We relied on freelance contracts, which meant most contributors worked part-time, often on evenings and weekends. That slowed us down — but it also gave us access to talented professionals from major studios, who wouldn’t have been available under a traditional staffing model.

We built the game in the Godot engine, mainly because it’s open-source and produces lightweight builds — which we hoped would make future mobile ports easier (a plan that ultimately didn’t materialize). As our CTO and designer Maciej Stańczyk put it:

[i]Technically speaking, Godot’s a solid tool — but porting is a pain. For this project, I’d still choose it. But if you’re thinking beyond PC, you need to plan carefully.[/i]

Over the course of production, around 15 people contributed in some capacity. Most worked on narrowly defined tasks — like creating a few specific animations. About 10 were involved intermittently, while the core team consisted of about five people who carried the project forward. Of those, only one — our CEO and lead writer Jędrzej Napiecek — worked on the game full-time. The rest balanced it with other jobs.

We ran the project entirely remotely. In hindsight, it was the only viable option. Renting a physical studio would’ve burned through our budget in a matter of months. And for a game like this — long on writing, short on gameplay mechanics — full-time roles weren’t always necessary. A full-time programmer, for instance, would’ve spent much of the project waiting for things to script. Given the constraints, we think the budget was spent as efficiently as possible.

[h1]Marketing and Wishlists[/h1]

For the first leg of the marketing campaign, we handled everything ourselves — posting regularly on Reddit, Facebook, and Twitter. Between July and October 2022, those grassroots efforts brought in around 1,000 wishlists. Modest, but promising. During that period, we took part in Steam Next Fest — a decision we later came to regret. Sure, our wishlist count doubled, but we were starting from such a low base that the absolute numbers were underwhelming. In hindsight, we would’ve seen a much bigger impact if we had joined the event closer to launch, when our wishlist count was higher and the game had more visibility.

Then, in November 2022, our publisher came on board. Within just two days, our wishlist count jumped by 2,000. It looked impressive — at first. They told us the spike came from mailing list campaigns. But when we dug into the data, we found something odd: the vast majority of those wishlists came from Russia. Actual sales in that region? Just a few dozen copies... We still don’t know what really happened — whether it was a mailing list fluke, a bot issue, or something else entirely. But the numbers didn’t add up, and that initial spike never translated into meaningful engagement. You can see that spike here - it’s the biggest one:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/15ff90294a2ae3de95d1d1144caa00911fe8d76b.jpg[/img]

From there, wishlist growth slowed. Over the next six months — the lead-up to launch — we added about 1,000 more wishlists. To put it bluntly: in four months of DIY marketing, we’d done about as well as the publisher did over half a year. Not exactly a glowing endorsement.

That said, the launch itself went reasonably well. The publisher managed to generate some nice visibility, generating about 50K visits on our Steam Page on the day of the premiere.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/03915c2d45a56f6e274279968bd85cf8e34ed465.jpg[/img]

You can compare it to our lifetime results - we managed to gather 12.33 million impressions and 1,318,116 visits of our Steam Page during both marketing and sales phases:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/4d2055043bebe84950ca02c6155febbaea282af9.jpg[/img]

It’s worth noting that nearly 50 titles launched on Steam the same day we did. Among them, we managed to climb to the #3 spot in terms of popularity. A small victory, sure — but one that highlights just how fierce the competition is on the platform. 

Looking back, the launch may not have delivered blockbuster sales, but it did well enough to keep the game from vanishing into the depths of Steam’s archive. It’s still alive, still visible, and — to our mild surprise — still selling, if slowly.

After the premiere we saw a healthy bump: roughly 2,500 new wishlists in the month following release. By early June 2023, our total had climbed to around 6,300. After that, growth was slower but steady. We crossed the 10,000-wishlist mark in May 2024, a full year after launch. Since then, things have tapered off. Over the past twelve months, we’ve added just 1,500 more wishlists. Here are our actual wishlist stats:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/3f16618e5280223b55f81f83cb533dd1af7546dc.jpg[/img]

During the promotional period, we also visited many in-person events: EGX London, PAX East Boston, GDC San Francisco, BLON Klaipeda. We managed to obtain the budget for these trips - mostly - from additional grants for the international development of the company. And while these trips allowed us to establish interesting industry contacts, the impact on wish lists was negligible. In our experience - it is better to invest money in online marketing than to pay for expensive stands at fairs.

[h1]Sales[/h1]

Two years post-launch, We. The Refugees has [b]sold 3,653 copies [/b]— plus around 259 retail activations — with 211 refunds. That’s a 5.8% refund rate, and [b]an average of about five sales per day [/b]since release.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/eeda8d750368f8a4f957948db891d512901ccdc1.jpg[/img]

China turned out to be our biggest market by far, accounting for 46% of all sales. The credit goes entirely to our Chinese partner, Gamersky, who handled localization and regional distribution. They did outstanding work — not just on the numbers, but on communication, responsiveness, and professionalism. Partnering with them was, without question, one of our best decisions. Our second-largest market was the U.S. at 16%, followed by Poland at 6%. That last figure might seem surprising, but we need to highlight that Act Zero is a Polish studio and the game is fully localized in Polish.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/6168c91fb14b913ba7f9805f91e1efc465ba56e5.jpg[/img]

Looking at our daily sales chart, the pattern is clear: most purchases happen during Steam festivals or seasonal sales. Outside of those events, daily numbers drop sharply — often to near-zero. As of now, our lifetime conversion rate sits at 10.7%, slightly below the Steam average.

We haven’t yet tested ultra-deep discounts (like -90%), which may still offer some upside. But for now, the game’s long tail is exactly what you'd expect from a niche, dialogue-heavy title without a major marketing push.

Initially, we had higher hopes. We believed 10,000 copies in the first year was a realistic target. But a mix of limited marketing, creative risks, and production compromises made that goal harder to reach. In the next section, we’ll try to unpack what exactly went wrong — and what we’d do differently next time.


[h1]Mistakes & Lessons Learned[/h1]

[list]
[*] [b]No Map or True Exploration [/b]
[/list]
[i]We. The Refugees[/i] is a game about a journey from North Africa to Southern Europe — yet ironically, the game lacks the feeling of freedom and movement that such a journey should evoke. The player follows a mostly linear, pre-scripted route with some branches along the way. The main route of the journey is more or less the same, although there are different ways of exploring specific sections of the route. Even a simple map with optional detours could’ve dramatically improved immersion. Moving gameplay choices about the next destination onto such a map would also be highly recommended — it would definitely liven up interactions on the left side of the screen, where illustrations are displayed. Clicking on them would simply offer a refreshing change from the usual dialogue choices shown beneath the text on the right side of the screen. After all, the “journey” is a powerful narrative and gameplay topos — one that many players find inherently engaging. Unfortunately, our game didn’t reflect this in its systems or structure.

[list]
[*] [b]Too Little Gameplay, Too Much Reading[/b]
[/list]
Players didn’t feel like they were actively participating — and in a modern RPG or visual novel, interactivity is key. Introducing simple mechanics, like dice checks during major decisions or a basic quest log, would’ve helped structure the action and add dramatic tension. These are familiar tools that players have come to expect, and we shouldn't have overlooked them.

[list]
[*] [b]Personality Traits with No Real Impact[/b]
[/list]
The player character had a set of personality traits, but they were largely cosmetic. Occasionally, a trait would unlock a unique dialogue option, but in practice, these had little to no impact on how the story unfolded. We missed a major opportunity here. Traits could have formed the backbone of a dice-based gameplay system, where they meaningfully influenced outcomes by providing bonuses or penalties to specific checks — adding depth, variety, and replay value.

[list]
[*] [b]Mispositioned Pitch[/b]
[/list]
From the start, we positioned the game as a story about refugees — a highly politicized topic that immediately turned away many potential players. Some assumed we were pushing propaganda. But our actual intent was far more nuanced: we tried to show the refugee issue from multiple perspectives, without preaching or moralizing — trusting players to draw their own conclusions from the situations we presented.

Looking back, a better framing would’ve been: a young journalist’s first investigative assignment — which happens to deal with refugees. This would’ve made the game far more approachable. The refugee theme could remain central, but framed as part of a broader, more relatable fantasy of becoming a journalist.

[list]
[*] [b]A Problematic Protagonist[/b]
[/list]
We aimed to create a non-heroic protagonist — not a hardened war reporter, but an ordinary person, similar to the average player. Someone unprepared, naive, flawed. Our goal was to satirize the Western gaze, but many players found this portrayal alienating. It was hard to empathize with a character who often made dumb mistakes or revealed glaring ignorance.

The idea itself wasn’t bad — challenging the “cool protagonist” fantasy can be powerful — but we executed it clumsily. We gave the main character too many flaws, to the point where satire and immersion clashed. A better approach might’ve been to delegate those satirical traits to a companion character, letting the player avatar stay more neutral. As our CTO Maciej Stańczyk put it:

[i]I still think a protagonist who’s unlikable at first isn’t necessarily a bad idea — but you have to spell it out clearly, because players are used to stepping into the shoes of someone cool right away.[/i]

[list]
[*][b] A Static, Uninviting Prologue[/b]
[/list]
The game’s prologue begins with the protagonist sitting in his apartment, staring at a laptop (starting conditions exactly the same as the situation of our player right now!), moments before leaving for Africa. On paper, it seemed clever — metatextual, symbolic. In practice, it was static and uninvolving. Many players dropped the game during this segment.

Ironically, the very next scene — set in Africa — was widely praised as engaging and atmospheric. In hindsight, we should’ve opened in medias res, grabbing the player’s attention from the first few minutes. Again, Maciej Stańczyk summed it up well:

[i]The prologue is well-written and nicely sets up the character, but players expect a hook in the first few minutes — like starting the story right in the middle of the action.[/i]

[list]
[*] [b]No Saving Option[/b]
[/list]
The decision to disable saving at any moment during gameplay turned out to be a mistake. Our intention was to emphasize the weight of each choice and discourage save scumming. However, in practice, it became a frustrating limitation—especially for our most dedicated and engaged players, who wanted to explore different narrative branches but were repeatedly forced to replay large portions of the game.

[list]
[*] [b]Late and Weak Marketing[/b]
[/list]
We started marketing way too late. We had no budget for professionals and little expertise ourselves. We tried to learn on the fly, but lacked time, resources, and experience. What we could have done better was involve the community much earlier. As Maciej Stańczyk notes:

[i]Biggest lesson? Involve your community as early as possible. Traditional marketing only works if you’ve got at least a AA+ budget. Indies have to be loud and visible online from the earliest stages — like the guy behind Roadwarden, whose posts I saw years before launch.[/i]

[b]Final Thoughts on Mistakes[/b]

If we were to start this project all over again, two priorities would guide our design: more interactive gameplay and freedom to explore the journey via a world map. Both would significantly increase immersion and player engagement.

Could we have achieved that with the budget we had? Probably not. But that doesn’t change the fact that now we know better — and we intend to apply those lessons to our next project.

[h1]Closing Thoughts[/h1]

Two years after launch, we’re proud of how [i]We. The Refugees[/i] has been received. The game holds an 83% positive rating on Steam and has earned nominations and awards at several international festivals. We won Games for Good Award at IndieX in Portugal, received a nomination to Best in Civics Award at Games for Change in New York, and another to Aware Game Awards at BLON in Lithuania. For a debut indie title built on a shoestring budget, that’s not nothing.

We’re also proud of the final product itself. Despite some narrative missteps, we believe the writing holds up — both in terms of quality and relevance. As the years go by, the game may even gain value as a historical snapshot of a particular state of mind. The story ends just as the COVID-19 lockdowns begin — a moment that, in hindsight, marked the end of a certain era. In the five years since, history has accelerated. The comfortable notion of the “End of History” (to borrow from Fukuyama) — so common in Western discourse — has given way to a harsher, more conflict-driven reality. In that context, our protagonist might be seen as a portrait of a fading worldview. A symbol of the mindset that once shaped liberal Western optimism, now slipping into obsolescence. And perhaps that alone is reason enough for the game to remain interesting in the years to come — as a kind of time capsule, a record of a specific cultural moment.

This reflection also marks the closing of a chapter for our studio. While we still have a few surprises in store for [i]We. The Refugees[/i], our attention has already shifted to what lies ahead. We’re now putting the finishing touches on the prototype for [i]Venus Rave[/i] — a sci-fi RPG with a much stronger gameplay core (which, let’s be honest, wasn’t hard to improve given how minimal gameplay was in [i]We. The Refugees[/i]). The next phase of development still lacks a secured budget, but thanks to everything we’ve learned on our first project, we’re walking into this one better prepared — and determined not to repeat the same mistakes.

Whether we get to make that next game depends on whether someone out there believes in us enough to invest. Because - being completely honest - the revenue from our first title won’t be enough to fund another one on its own.

So, here's our take on our debut title from a distance. And what do you think about [i]We. The Refugees[/i], two years after its release?

notes.title: Charity Donations & Bunch of Exciting News!
notes.notes:
Hey, gamers!

It’s been a while since our last update, but that’s because we’ve been fully focused on developing the prototype for our next game! The good news? The prototype is almost complete, which means we can finally take a moment to revisit our previous title.

And we’re coming back with some great news!

First and foremost—just like every year around this time—we’ve made our annual donations to our friends and partners at [b]Hope Project[/b] and [b]Fundacja Ocalenie[/b]. We’ve just transferred 5% of 2024 game’s profits to support their charity work. And here’s something really exciting—this year’s donation was even bigger than last year’s! That’s all thanks to you, and we truly appreciate your support!

Secondly, we want to apologize for the delay in releasing the Mac version of the game. Our small team had to shift focus to our new project for a while, which slowed things down. But the good news is that we don’t have much work left to do before it’s ready, and we hope to get back to it soon!

Lastly, let’s talk about [b]our new game[/b]. We’ve successfully secured funding for the prototype, and that phase of development is now complete! We still need a little more time to refine things before we can share a sneak peek with you. But what we can tell you is that some official announcements are coming! Once again, we’re diving into the world of [b]interactive fiction[/b], but this time with more RPG mechanics. And while we’ll continue tackling ambitious themes, this time we’ll be exploring modern issues from a unique angle—through the lens of the future. And all that in the rythms of electronic beats...

We don't want to reveal too many details yet, but... we can't help ourselves! Just look at this concept art :)

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/05003e5f496324230d7eddbd18f00375d5e24f62.jpg[/img]

Do you already have any ideas what our next game will be about? And in general: How are you doing? :)

Best wishes to all of ya,
Act Zero team

notes.title: We have been nominated for the G4C Awards!
notes.notes:
We are happy to announce that [b]we have been nominated for the G4C Awards[/b] as one of three games in the category: Best in Civics!

Games For Change is one of the most important festivals in the world that brings together socially engaged, impactful games. When creating "We. The Refugees", we aimed at exactly such audiences, so being nominated at such a festival - and with our first game - is a real dream come true.

The G4C Festival will take place from June 27 to June 28, 2024 and you can participate in it in person if you go to the festival in New York :) More details about this can be found on: [url=https://www.gamesforchange.org/]G4C website[/url] 

Keep your fingers crossed for us on June 27, because that's when the Awards Ceremony will take place. 

We also encourage you to check out the other nominated games, because there are a lot of great and important titles there.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/42714089/2dad0937b14f6755adf0b42bdf1b5bfc00feac0f.png[/img]

notes.title: -50% discount on the 1st Anniversary of the Release
notes.notes:
Hello people!

May marked the first year since the release of We. The Refugees.

On this occasion, we [b]have prepared a two-week long and the highest discount so far, reaching up to -50%![/b]

During this period, we are also taking part in two events on Steam: One of them is Polish Constitution Days, and the other one... we will announce it soon :)

It's amazing that a year has passed since the release of our first game. During this time, we managed to sell 1,295 copies of the game, which translates into approximately 4 copies a day. It may not be a very large number, but we are extremely happy that we are still able to reach new players, and the reviews are mostly positive. We are pleased with the reception of the story in our game, and at the same time we have a lot of thoughts on what to do to make the next games better. We definitely want to invest more resources in expanding gameplay elements and mechanics known from RPG games to make our next game (which we are already working on!) a more interactive experience. Also expect more world exploration elements! There will still be time to announce the new title, and in the meantime we would like to thank our wonderful community for supporting us and being with us in our attempt to tell an ambitious story in games. Thanks to your involvement, we also manage to support charitable purposes in the form of NGOs with which we will continue cooperation.

Thanks again for all the kind words and take care!

notes.title: End of cooperation with the publisher
notes.notes:
As of January 1, 2024, we officially ended our cooperation with our current publisher, Polyslash S. A. 

We are grateful for the year of cooperation and all the marketing support that Polyslash provided us. 

[b]Starting from January 1, Act Zero becomes not only a developer, but also a publisher of "We. The Refugees: Ticket to Europe"[/b]. We take full responsibility for the continued operation of this title and will try to correct any mistakes made previously. We are sad to inform that the declared amount of 5% support for charitable purposes - with the exception of profits from the first two months after launch - was not realized due to not receiving payments that we have been owed. However, good sales results in December and the fact that we regained control over money transfers from Steam will allow us to cover outstanding amounts due to charity at the turn of January and February 2024, and we commit to doing so.

Today we are starting a New Year and with it a new beginning in our business.

All the best for all our players and followers in 2024! Thank you for all your support so far. And if you want to help us on our new path, we encourage you to consider purchasing our game, taking advantage of the -33% reduced price (only for a few more days!) and the fact that this time the money will 100% go to us :)

Wish us luck! It's going to be an exciting year!

Sincerely,
[i]Act Zero team[/i]

PS: As a part of our renewed efforts to keep "We. The Refugees" alive, we are currently working on yet another patch - you can expect it in very near future!

notes.title: Chances are small, but it's still worth a try...
notes.notes:
The Steam Nomination Awards starts today and the competition is massive and our game is a really a niche one, but... It still it's worth a try, isn't it?

If you think it is worth appreciating our efforts:
[list]
[*] five years of research and struggle to create this game without any budget
[*] 3 years of actual gamedevelopment
[*] giving a voice to actual refugees and volunteers with whom we consulted the script
[*] writing a 300,000-word script with thousands of dialogue choices and branching narratives... 
[/list]
...then we would be extremely grateful if you voted for [b]"We. The Refugees: Ticket to Europe"[/b] in the category:

[b]Outstanding Story-Rich Games[/b]

We realize that there is a 99.99% chance that we will not win, but your vote would not be wasted as it would mean a lot for us. It would be a sign that you appreciate our working methods, in which we try to present complicated and important subjects in an attractive and in-depth way. We do not take shortcuts and do not follow trends, but we simply try to present good, engaging stories on difficult and important topics without manipulating facts and without suggesting top-down conclusions, because we believe in the intelligence of our players and their ability to form their own opinions...

notes.title: We. The Refugees at ChinaJoy live event!
notes.notes:
We were very lucky at the beginning of this year. 

Thanks to some random Twitter interaction, we met Brandon from Gamersky, who publishes games in China. Brandon offered to cooperate in this market and localize the game to Chinese. Indie studios receive hundreds of such messages and usually nothing comes of it. Also, our game had an inappropriately long script, so we didn't really believe that someone would undertake the translation only a few months before launch. But Gamersky took up this challenge. And not only did they manage to translate 300,000 words in several weeks, but they also became our ambassador among Chinese-speaking players. And in a very effective way, because after 3 months from the release, Chinese players are our largest percentage on Steam! 

And now, in addition, Brandon has gone to China's biggest gaming festival known as ChinaJoy, where you can find a booth with We. The Refugees! The inscrutable power of the internet continues to amaze us. 

Thanks, Gamersky, for everything! And we encourage all Chinese players to check out We. The Refugees at ChinaJoy! The festival starts today (28.07.2023)  and runs until Monday (31.07.2023).

notes.title: Devs to Players: After-Premiere Appreciation Post
notes.notes:
It's been a full week since the premiere of "We. The Refugees" - it was quite a surreal experience for us: after so many years of work, we thought that the day of the premiere would never come... But we made it :)

[b]And we are extremely grateful for the supportive feedback we receive from you.[/b] Well over 90% of the feedback we receive from players is positive! It's amazing because we've made a game that actually...shouldn't work because:

[list]
[*] deals with a very difficult and delicate subject
[*] presents this topic from a controversial perspective, because it is balanced and presents a very wide spectrum of opinions on the portrayed subject
[*] the game is overwhelmingly text-based in a time when literature is dying
[*] its a seemingly uncomplicated game in a rather niche genre
[*] and therefore requiring patience and time to discover its complexity and hidden mechanics
[/list]

And yet you want to play our game! It's amazing and... incomprehensible to us ;)

Plus, [b]we're thrilled to see so many people actually play the game:[/b] 78% of players have completed the prologue and unlocked the first note from Egypt, and over 50% have reached Act 2. Wow! You really want to explore the world we've created.

However, you haven't discovered everything yet! [b]Although the game has been online for 7 days, you still haven't discovered all the hidden paths and content[/b]: No one has yet learned the full story of the Syrian nurse Almas, the story of Dinah's stump, or experienced the paradoxes of egoism... Only about 1% of you ended up in prison during your adventures (yes, it's possible!), or... experienced stomach indigestion during a storm ;). We take it as a compliment that we created such a complex and full of hidden scenes story that you still have a lot to discover after a week of playing :)

[b]Thank you all - this gives us hope that creating ambitious and complex narratives in games makes sense and motivates us to continue working in this direction. [/b]And each copy of the game you buy is a small step towards the next, even more extensive and complex game for which we already have an idea :)

However, to all those still hesitating whether it is worth playing "We. The Refugees" - we would like to remind you that [b]for 3 more days you can do it at a reduced price, thanks to the premiere discount -10%. [/b]The discount ends on May 11, and you will have to wait a while for the next promotion! :)

Best wishes everyone,
Act Zero Team

2. We wrote descriptions of tags and items
3. We wrote the texts for the achievements and created the design of their icons
4. We updated the credits

9. We've made some adjustments to the settings
10. We tested the game dozens of times

notes.title: Why a video game at all? / DEVLOG#3
notes.notes:
In the early stages of development, we often encountered misunderstandings and doubts:

"If you are so interested in refugees, if their fate is on your heart, why do you want to make a video game about them? And not - for example - a documentary movie or a literary reportage?", people asked, "Refugee stories have already been told in these media - and with success.[b] But the game? It seems like an inappropriate medium to tell such a story.[/b]"

And although these doubts made sense, for us it was just another argument to talk about refugees through the medium of video games. Precisely because few people have tried it before.

It seems to us that people interested in literary reportages and documentaries have already found relevant cultural works about refugees and knew the subject well enough. On the other hand, players still haven't had many opportunities to look at the subject of refugees through their favorite medium. It seemed to us (and still seems to be) one of the greatest values ​​of our project: it is a chance to reach a new and as wide audience as possible with our message (which - as we will probably write about in some future devlogs - is not propaganda at all, as many commentators suggests).

At a later stage of development, some doubted whether a video game would allow us to present the full complexity of the refugee issue. Our answer is simple: 

"We read about 30-40 books about refugees, watched a lot of doc movies, visited a refugee camp on our own, talked with them and also with volunteers, and we consulted each of the 1,200 pages of the script with subject matter experts from NGOs and reporters. If it is possible to present the world of refugees in 400 pages of reportage or 90 minutes doc, it is also possible in the 1,200 pages of scenario of our game (which translates to about 30 hours of content in total)."

Even more! In our opinion, [b]a video game is just a perfect medium to tell the story of refugees[/b]. Its interactive nature and natural immersion allows players to engage more deeply with the topic presented. The fundamental mechanics of our game is making choices (and struggling with consequences). It is a much more engaging way of absorbing content than passive reading or watching a movie. Here, the player really is part of the adventure and really needs to think about his opinion on the difficult issues that the game presents to him. It is a way of learning to think independently, and not to force the recipient into the head of already-made conclusions.

notes.title: The genesis of 'Ticket to Europe' / DEVLOG#2
notes.notes:
Hello, people! 

Today, a few words about the genesis of 'Ticket to Europe'.

The idea to create a game about refugees appeared in 2014. It was the very beginning of the so-called "migration crisis" and the media was just beginning to get interested in this topic.

Our Lead Writer, Jędrzej Napiecek, came across a short article about people who tried to cross the Mediterranean Sea on board of simple boats to get to Europe from Africa. This deeply touched him emotionally and he wondered: What mental condition do you need to be in order to recognize that a better choice at the moment would be a trip on a poor boat or pontoon across a huge sea than staying on the often heavenly African beach, to which many people go to vacation?

The thought had haunted him for months, and he finally decided to try to find an answer to that question the only way he knew: by writing a script about it.

At the time of making this decision, he was already in the process of changing the industry (from cinema to gamedev) and worked as a game tester on 'The Witcher 3', where he met our Game Designer, Maciej Stańczyk. They both shared common interests and ideals - they wanted to create ambitious video games that would be not only entertainment, but also an artistic expression on important, contemporary topics. And the socially involved subject of refugees - which touched them emotionally - seemed to be the perfect choice for their first, common game.

They decided that Jędrzej would write a game script about refugees, Maciej would design the game mechanics, and then they would create the game together. They didn't suspect that this process would take so many years, but that's a topic for a separate devlog.
